For every smooth real-valued Hamiltonian \(H\in C^\infty((\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times M)\), write \(H_t=H(t,\cdot)\), define its vector field by \(\omega(X_{H_t},\cdot)=d_MH_t\), and let \(\varphi_H^1\) be the evolution map from time \(0\) to time \(1\) of \(\dot x=X_{H_t}(x)\). Here \(d_M\) denotes differentiation in the spatial variable.

Among all such Hamiltonians for which \(\operatorname{Fix}(\varphi_H^1)=\{x\in M:\varphi_H^1(x)=x\}\) is finite, determine the minimum possible number of distinct fixed points. Count each fixed point once, without multiplicity; no invertibility condition is imposed on \(D\varphi_H^1(x)-I\) at a fixed point.
</problem>

7	The allowance of degenerate fixed points is essential. We prove the lower bound, then construct a smooth function with exactly three critical points and explain why a sufficiently small autonomous Hamiltonian generated by it has exactly three fixed points.
8	
9	## 1. The lower bound
10	
11	We use the classical **degenerate Arnold–Floer cup-length theorem** in its monotone form:
12	
13	> Let \(X^{2n}\) be closed and positively monotone, with minimal Chern number \(N\ge n\). A Hamiltonian diffeomorphism with finitely many fixed points has at least
14	> \[
15	> 1+\operatorname{cuplength}_{\mathbb F_2}(X)
16	> \]
17	> distinct fixed points. Nondegeneracy of the fixed points is not required.
18	
19	Here, writing \(A=[S^2\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}]\) and \(B=[\{\mathrm{pt}\}\times S^2]\), we have
20	\[
21	\omega(A)=\omega(B)=4\pi,\qquad c_1(A)=c_1(B)=2.
22	\]
23	Thus
24	\[
25	[\omega]=2\pi c_1\quad\text{on }\pi_2(M),
26	\]
27	and \(N=2=n\).
28	
29	Furthermore,
30	\[
31	H^*(M;\mathbb F_2)
32	 =\mathbb F_2[a,b]/(a^2,b^2),\qquad |a|=|b|=2.
33	\]
34	Since \(ab\ne0\), its cup length is two. Consequently,
35	\[
36	\#\operatorname{Fix}(\varphi_H^1)\ge3.
37	\]
38	
39	This standard Floer theorem is the only deep fixed-point theorem used below.
40	
41	## 2. A smooth function with exactly three critical points
42	
43	We give the construction, including the local replacement that merges two critical points.
44	
45	Start with
46	\[
47	h(x,y)=x_3+y_3.
48	\]
49	It has four critical points: its maximum, its minimum, and the two index-two points
50	\[
51	p=(N,S),\qquad q=(S,N).
52	\]
53	Both middle critical points lie in \(h^{-1}(0)\). They are connected in that level by the embedded arc
54	\[
55	\gamma(\theta)=
56	\bigl((\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta),
57	      (\sin\theta,0,-\cos\theta)\bigr),
58	\qquad 0\le\theta\le\pi.
59	\]
60	The interior of this arc consists of regular points of \(h\).
61	
62	### 2.1 Coordinates around the arc
63	
64	There are coordinates \((u,v,s,t)\) on a neighborhood of this arc in which
65	\[
66	\gamma=\{(u,0,0,0):0\le u\le L\},
67	\qquad
68	h=A(u)v+st,                                      \tag{1}
69	\]
70	where \(A\) is positive on \((0,L)\), equals \(u\) near \(0\), and equals \(L-u\) near \(L\). In particular, \(A<0\) just outside \([0,L]\).
71	
72	Here are details ensuring this normal form.
73	
74	Near \(p=(N,S)\), introduce smooth coordinates
75	\[
76	(P_i,Q_i)=\frac{(x_{i,1},x_{i,2})}{\sqrt{1+|x_{i,3}|}}
77	\]
78	on the respective sphere factors. They give
79	\[
80	h=P_2^2+Q_2^2-P_1^2-Q_1^2.
81	\]
82	Along the indicated arc, \(P_1=P_2\ge0\) and \(Q_1=Q_2=0\). Therefore, setting
83	\[
84	u=P_2+P_1,\quad v=P_2-P_1,\quad
85	s=Q_2+Q_1,\quad t=Q_2-Q_1
86	\]
87	gives exactly
88	\[
89	h=uv+st
90	\]
91	and makes the arc the positive \(u\)-axis. The same construction, with the factors reversed, works at \(q\).
92	
93	On the regular interior of the arc, extend the coordinates \(u,s,t\) from these endpoint charts so that
94	\[
95	(du,dh,ds,dt)
96	\]
97	is a coframe. This is the relative tubular-neighborhood construction along an interval: the relevant rank-two transverse bundle is trivial. If necessary, interchange \(s,t\) at one endpoint to match the framing; this preserves \(st\). Choose \(A>0\) in the interior with the stated endpoint values and define
98	\[
99	v=\frac{h-st}{A(u)}.
100	\]
101	This agrees with the endpoint coordinates on their overlaps. Shrinking the neighborhood gives the single embedded coordinate neighborhood asserted in (1).

103	### 2.2 A ball around the arc with a useful outward field
104	
105	On a slightly larger interval than \([0,L]\), put
106	\[
107	d(u)=
108	\begin{cases}
109	e^{-1/u^2},&u<0,\\
110	0,&0\le u\le L,\\
111	e^{-1/(u-L)^2},&u>L.
112	\end{cases}
113	\]
114	Define
115	\[
116	D=d(u)+v^2+s^2+t^2.
117	\]
118	For sufficiently small \(\delta>0\),
119	\[
120	U=\{D\le\delta\}
121	\]
122	is a smooth four-ball contained in the coordinate neighborhood.
123	
124	For completeness, its boundary is smooth because \(\nabla D\) cannot vanish on \(D=\delta>0\). It is strictly star-shaped about any \((u_0,0,0,0)\), \(0<u_0<L\), since on its boundary
125	\[
126	\nabla D\cdot(u-u_0,v,s,t)
127	=d'(u)(u-u_0)+2(v^2+s^2+t^2)>0.
128	\]
129	Thus it is indeed a smoothly parametrized ball.
130	
131	Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) small enough that
132	\[
133	b(u)=1+\varepsilon A'(u)d'(u)>0,
134	\]
135	and set
136	\[
137	a(u)=-\varepsilon A(u)d'(u),\qquad
138	Y=a(u)\partial_u+b(u)v\partial_v

140	\]

144	\]

148	\]

150

154	\]

156	
157	The flow of \(Y\) supplies a collar, with coordinate \(\tau\le0\), on which (2) says exactly
158	\[
159	h(\tau,\theta)=e^\tau g(\theta).                         \tag{4}
160	\]
161	
162	### 2.3 Replace the two critical points by one flat critical point
163	
164	Parametrize \(\partial U\) by \(S^3\), using a parametrization extending over the ball \(U\). Replace the function inside this ball by the following radial function on a standard ball:
165	\[
166	F(r,\theta)=\psi(r)g(\theta),\qquad F(0)=0.
167	\]
168	Here \(\psi\) is smooth, positive and strictly increasing for \(r>0\), flat at zero, and equals \(r\) near \(1\).
169	
170	An explicit choice is
171	\[
172	\psi(r)=r\exp\!\left(-\frac{\chi(r)}{r^2}\right),
173	\]
174	where \(\chi\) is smooth and nonincreasing, equals \(1\) for \(r\le1/2\), and equals \(0\) for \(r\ge3/4\). Indeed,
175	\[
176	\frac{\psi'(r)}{\psi(r)}
177	=\frac1r-\frac{\chi'(r)}{r^2}+\frac{2\chi(r)}{r^3}>0.
178	\]
179	Its flatness makes \(F\) smooth at the origin.
180	
181	There are no critical points for \(r>0\):
182	
183	* if \(g(\theta)\ne0\), then \(\partial_rF=\psi'(r)g(\theta)\ne0\);
184	* if \(g(\theta)=0\), then \(d_\theta F=\psi(r)\,dg(\theta)\ne0\).
185	
186	The origin is a critical point. Near the boundary, \(F=rg\); taking \(r=e^\tau\), this agrees with (4), so the replacement glues smoothly to \(h\) outside \(U\). Collar uniqueness allows this gluing to use the chosen ball parametrization.
187	
188	We have therefore constructed a smooth function \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) with precisely
189	\[
190	\boxed{\text{one minimum, one maximum, and one further critical point}.}
191	\]
192	The latter is highly degenerate.

194	## 3. Making its Hamiltonian flow slow
195	
196	We justify carefully that taking a small multiple of \(f\) creates no additional time-one fixed points.
197	
198	View \(M\subset\mathbb R^6\), and write \(X=X_f\). Smoothness and compactness imply that \(X:M\to\mathbb R^6\) has a finite ambient Lipschitz constant \(C\).
199	
200	Suppose a nonconstant \(T\)-periodic trajectory satisfies
201	\[
202	\dot x=\lambda X(x).
203	\]
204	Its mean velocity is zero, so \(\overline{X(x)}=0\). The variance identity and the Lipschitz inequality give
205	\[
206	\int_0^T |X(x(t))|^2\,dt
207	\le C^2\int_0^T|x(t)-\bar x|^2\,dt .
208	\]
209	Applying the periodic Wirtinger inequality,
210	\[
211	\int_0^T|x-\bar x|^2\,dt
212	\le\frac{T^2}{4\pi^2}\int_0^T|\dot x|^2\,dt ,
213	\]
214	and using \(\dot x=\lambda X(x)\), we obtain
215	\[
216	1\le\frac{\lambda^2C^2T^2}{4\pi^2}.
217	\]
218	Thus every nonconstant periodic trajectory has
219	\[
220	T\ge\frac{2\pi}{\lambda C}.
221	\]
222	
223	Choose \(\lambda>0\) with \(\lambda C<2\pi\), and set
224	\[
225	H(t,x)=\lambda f(x).
226	\]
227	There are no nonconstant one-periodic trajectories. Its time-one fixed points are therefore exactly the zeros of \(X_f\), equivalently the three critical points of \(f\).
